Quantum Computing Inc. Announces Dirac-3S, Scaling to Nearly 10,000 Variables
Thu, October 1, 2026 at 5:30 AM PDT 6 min read
Scales quantum optimization to up to nearly 10,000 variables, a 10x increase over QCi's current 1,000-variable system, while delivering faster performance, production-ready reliability and scalable manufacturing
First customer shipment of Dirac-3S upgrade expected in Q4 2026
HOBOKEN, N.J., Oct. 1, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Quantum Computing Inc. ("QCi" or the "Company") (Nasdaq: QUBT), a vertically integrated quantum systems company pioneering photonics and semiconductor manufacturing, today announced Dirac-3S, the next-generation of its Dirac-3 quantum optimization machine, marking a significant step toward commercial deployment of QCi's quantum optimization technology.
Dirac-3S advances the platform across three areas – Speed, Scale and Solutions – with faster performance, improved solution quality, increased computing capacity and a modular architecture designed to support customers as their requirements grow. The first customer shipment of Dirac-3S is expected in November 2026.
Speed. Scale. Solutions.
Speed: Dirac-3S is engineered to efficiently solve increasingly complex optimization problems, with practical computation times demonstrated on problems involving up to 9,980 variables while consistently finding the optimal solution. This enables customers to tackle larger problems and explore more possibilities in less time.
Scale: Dirac-3S features a modular architecture designed to scale with customer requirements. The compact 5U base system can be extended with Expansion Modules to support larger and more complex optimization problems, with QCi demonstrating configurations supporting up to 9,980 variables with one Expansion Module. The architecture is designed to accommodate additional Expansion Modules, enabling customers to expand their system as their optimization needs grow. QCi has also advanced the Dirac-3S hardware architecture, manufacturing processes and supply chain to support increased production volumes, consistent product quality and broader commercial deployment. These improvements include enhanced error correction, component control and operational reliability.
Solutions: Dirac-3S is designed to address a broad range of real-world optimization problems on a single platform, through multiple optimization approaches including continuous, integer and higher-order optimization. QCi's latest error-correction techniques are designed to improve solution quality across applications in financial services, logistics and supply chains, manufacturing, energy, telecommunications, scientific research, and aerospace and defense.
The platform can be deployed on-premises or in the cloud and integrated into AI/ML pipelines, enabling organizations to incorporate quantum optimization into existing computational workflows.
"Dirac-3S takes our quantum optimization platform from demonstrating what is possible to delivering a system built for practical commercial use," said Yong Meng Sua, Chief Technology Officer of QCi. "We have increased performance and computing capacity, expanded the size and complexity of problems the system can address through a modular architecture, and advanced the hardware and manufacturing architecture needed to support broader deployment. This gives customers a flexible path to adopt quantum optimization and scale their computing capacity as their needs grow."
Dirac-3S builds on QCi's first-generation Dirac-3 quantum optimization machine, which has been used by academic researchers exploring quantum optimization algorithms and applications.
"Our experience with the first-generation Dirac-3 quantum optimization machine validated its potential as a powerful tool for solving meaningful optimization problems. QCi's continued innovation with the Dirac-3S, including its expanded computational capabilities, enables us to pursue significantly larger and more complex optimization challenges. We look forward to exploring new research directions and accelerating the development of practical, high-impact applications," said Professor Paul Griffin, Associate Professor, Singapore Management University.
QCi has published a new Technical Review evaluating Dirac-3S across synthetic, graph-based and industry-standard optimization benchmarks, including comparisons with Projected Gradient Descent and commercial classical solver Hexaly. On synthetic problems with known global optima ranging from 2,000 to 9,980 variables, Dirac-3S was the only evaluated solver to achieve the optimal solution across all tested instances, while solution times increased only modestly as problem size approached 9,980 variables. On industry-standard DIMACS maximum-clique benchmarks, Dirac-3S more frequently identified the highest-quality solutions than the other evaluated methods.
QCi has also published a survey paper demonstrating how NP-hard problems can be mapped to simplex formulations native to Dirac-3S, expanding its potential applications across continuous, discrete and combinatorial optimization. The Technical Review, along with the detailed benchmarking methodology and results is available in QCi's Dirac-3S Technical Reference at: https://quantumcomputinginc.com/learn/module/dirac-3s-technical-reference.
To learn more about the Dirac-3S, visit QCi's Dirac-3S webpage.

(Nasdaq: QUBT) is a vertically integrated quantum systems company pioneering photonics and semiconductor manufacturing, and delivering accessible, scalable, and cost-effective quantum machines, photonics products, and advanced packaging. The Company provides foundry services for photonic chips and semiconductor manufacturing and offers a vertically integrated portfolio spanning photonics and electronic components, subsystems, and full-stack systems.
Designed to operate at room-temperature with low-power requirements, QCi's technologies enable practical deployment across high-growth markets, including high-performance computing, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, aerospace and defense, and advanced sensing and imaging.
Headquartered in Hoboken, New Jersey, QCi also has operations in Arizona, California, Illinois, Indiana, Massachusetts, North Carolina and Virginia. By combining advanced materials, device engineering, and scalable manufacturing, QCi delivers integrated quantum, photonics, and semiconductor technologies, accelerating commercialization and real-world adoption.

Quantum Computing Inc. (QUBT -2.93%) has gone from a little-known quantum computing stock to a company trying to build a real hardware business around photonics, semiconductor manufacturing, and quantum security. Its revenue growth suggests that customers are beginning to show up, but it's still losing money and asking investors to bet on an ambitious strategy that will be costly and difficult to execute.
Here's where the company, also known as QCi, stands today, what it is trying to build, and why the opportunity comes with considerable risk.

Quantum Computing Inc. describes itself as a "vertically integrated quantum company" built around photonics and semiconductor manufacturing, not just software or cloud access to quantum computers. It's listed on the Nasdaq and has moved from almost no revenue in 2025 to revenues of a few million dollars per quarter in 2026, but it still reports meaningful losses.
In its second‑quarter release, the company highlighted revenue of $5.6 million, up from $61,000 in the same quarter last year, but a net loss of $11.8 million. The top-line growth shows that QCi is no longer just a pre‑commercial story, but the bottom-line losses remind you that this business is still spending heavily to develop its technology and get its manufacturing platform off the ground.
Image source: Getty Images.
The more interesting part of QCi's story lives outside the income statement. The company has been assembling a stack that runs from photonic chips in a fab to full quantum computers and security platforms, as the TechJournal.uk Substack details. It has been doing this largely through a series of acquisitions such as NHanced Semiconductors and other photonics and packaging businesses. Management's "vertically integrated" language reflects the fact that QCi wants to control the critical pieces of quantum computing hardware (think chips, components, and packaging), rather than simply renting time on someone else's machines.
What I have my eyes on is the product side. QCi has announced NeuraWave, a photonic computing platform meant to handle real‑time AI inference at the edge. In other words, it's building hardware that can run complex models close to where data is generated rather than in distant data centers. It also showed off a quantum security system at the ECOC 2026 trade show that could help telecom companies keep their fiber networks safe. The bigger point is that quantum technology is starting to look less like a science project and more like something companies can actually deploy for commercially meaningful uses.
The problem, in my view, is that QCi is trying to do a lot of hard things at once: scale up its manufacturing, integrate multiple acquisitions, sell new classes of hardware, and educate customers on how to use quantum security and photonic computing. And it's doing all of these things while it's still losing money. That's a lot of execution risk, particularly for a stock that has a history of volatile and sentiment‑driven price moves. It's easy to be bearish about QCi; there isn't much revenue, and its heavy spending and reliance on secondary stock sales to raise operating capital make its current valuation hard to justify.
There's also competitive risk. Quantum computing hardware, quantum security, and edge AI are all crowded spaces, and QCi hasn't yet shown large, recurring deployments at the scale you'd want to see before calling it a durable growth story. Its recent revenue ramp-up is encouraging, but that growth came off an extremely small base, and investors have to assume that more capital spending, more technical risk, and more time will be needed before the company's platform will be mature.
If you're fascinated by quantum hardware and photonics and you accept that this is still a high‑risk, high‑uncertainty space, QCi might be worth a spot on your watch list or in the "small, experimental slice" of a diversified portfolio.

IonQ shares climbed approximately 14% in premarket trading following disclosure of a quantum error correction advancement.
Both Rigetti and D-Wave posted gains of roughly 6% as positive sentiment swept through quantum computing equities.
IonQ’s decoder underwent testing with as many as 408 logical qubits and over 31.5 million quantum operations.
Both Rigetti and D-Wave have recently obtained new federal funding commitments and collaborative research partnerships.
The Quantum World Congress 2026 kicks off Wednesday, highlighting commercialization pathways and government involvement.
Quantum computing equities climbed sharply during Wednesday’s premarket session following IonQ’s announcement of a significant technical achievement that energized the entire sector.
IonQ shares advanced approximately 14%, while both Rigetti Computing and D-Wave Quantum registered gains near 6%. This upward movement coincides with the opening of Quantum World Congress 2026 in Maryland, where industry leaders, federal representatives, and scientists are convening.
IonQ revealed what the company characterized as the industry’s first complete real-time quantum error correction decoder operating on conventional CPU hardware.
According to the company, testing spanned benchmark circuits incorporating up to 408 logical qubits and exceeding 31.5 million quantum operations. The system demonstrated processing overhead as low as 0.02%.
Addressing quantum error correction represents a critical hurdle for scaling quantum systems, as quantum computations exhibit extreme vulnerability to errors. IonQ’s methodology could potentially enable fault-tolerant architectures to expand without proportional growth in classical computing requirements.
This development arrives alongside a multi-year partnership with South Korea’s SDT. IonQ will deliver a Superion 256 quantum computer along with silicon-vacancy quantum memory modules, while both parties plan to establish a facility in Gumi dedicated to testing, integration, and packaging operations.
Rigetti and D-Wave Benefit from Industry Tailwinds
Rigetti shares climbed in tandem with IonQ following several recent federally supported initiatives.
The firm extended its collaboration with Hewlett Packard Enterprise and the Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center, committing to deliver a nine-qubit Novera system for a hybrid quantum-classical platform supported by a $5 million National Science Foundation grant.
Additionally, Rigetti recently secured a $100 million commitment from the U.S. Department of Commerce to advance superconducting quantum computing research and development efforts.
D-Wave registered approximately 6% gains after obtaining access to up to $100 million in support through the CHIPS and Science Act. The firm intends to allocate these resources toward superconducting annealing and gate-model quantum technologies.
D-Wave is anticipated to present on commercial and public-sector use cases throughout Quantum World Congress.
Market Analysts Track Quantum Sector Commercialization
Analyst perspectives remain generally constructive for all three companies, though price target projections exhibit considerable range.
IonQ carries an average analyst price target near $71 according to the referenced analysis, contrasting with Tuesday’s closing price around $41. Rigetti’s consensus target sits at approximately $29.50, while D-Wave’s stands near $35.79.
These projections suggest meaningful upside potential, though quantum computing stocks continue to demonstrate high volatility, with valuations heavily dependent on future technological breakthroughs and commercial adoption.
Wednesday’s rally demonstrates how rapidly investor enthusiasm can propagate throughout the sector when individual companies announce technical milestones. Market participants will now monitor Quantum World Congress closely for additional evidence that quantum computing is transitioning from laboratory research toward practical commercial applications.

IBM expands academic collaborations with IIT Bombay and IISc to advance Agentic AI, Sovereign AI, and quantum computing research
With IIT-B, IBM researchers will continue to work alongside faculty and students to explore sovereign and Indic language model adaption, multimodal AI, as well as AI infrastructure and knowledge retrieval.
IBM.
IBM has announced expansions of two long-standing research collaborations in India: one with the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Bombay, and another with the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) to accelerate innovation in agentic AI, sovereign AI, quantum computing and next-generation computing systems.
Building on a collaboration that began with IIT Bombay in 2018, IBM researchers will continue to work alongside faculty and students to explore sovereign and Indic language model adaption, multimodal AI, as well as AI infrastructure and knowledge retrieval. With IISc, IBM researchers will continue a collaboration that began in 2021, which covers agentic systems, AI for applications, and quantum computing algorithm development.
Strategic focus areas of IBM-IIT Bombay collaboration
Sovereign and Indic language model adaptation: Advancing sovereign AI and Indic language models to improve multilingual AI capabilities for Indian languages through more efficient model adaptation and optimization techniques.
Multimodal AI systems: The collaboration will also focus on developing multimodal AI systems that strengthen software programming education, human-AI collaboration and intelligent operations across hybrid cloud environments.
AI infrastructure and knowledge retrieval: Enhancing intelligent knowledge retrieval by developing AI systems that deliver faster, more accurate and scalable access to enterprise knowledge. The effort will be to optimize AI runtimes and distributed inference to improve the performance, efficiency and scalability of large language models.
Key pillars of IBM-IISc research collaboration
Agentic systems: Agentic AI workflows that improve orchestration across hybrid cloud environments, enabling more efficient management of AI applications while balancing performance, cost and operational complexity.
AI for scientific and industry applications: Creating lightweight time-series foundation models based on the IBM Granite model family for energy analytics to support forecasting, anomaly detection, load disaggregation and energy optimization, while contributing benchmark datasets to accelerate broader AI research.
Quantum computing: Exploring orchestration for quantum and high-performance computing to accelerate scientific discovery through more efficient quantum-centric supercomputing workflows and next-generation quantum-HPC algorithms. These algorithms would leverage approximation-tolerant classical diagonalization algorithms to improve quantum subspace iteration methods
Dr. Amith Singhee, Director, IBM Research India and CTO, IBM India and South Asia, said: "The next wave of computing will be shaped by advances in agentic AI, sovereign AI, and quantum computing. Our collaborations with IIT Bombay and IISc bring together world-class academic research and IBM's scientific expertise to solve some of the most complex challenges in these areas. Together, we are advancing research that not only pushes the boundaries of computing but also creates practical technologies that can benefit enterprises, developers and society."
Prof. Ganesh Ramakrishnan, Institute Chair Professor at the Department of Computer Science and Engineering, IIT Bombay, added: “The power of AI is already being demonstrated in systems that can seamlessly understand and reason across languages, modalities and domains. Our joint efforts with IBM Research are laying the foundation for such intelligent systems through advances in multimodal AI models, knowledge retrieval, optimization techniques, agentic AI workflows, AI-assisted software engineering and education.
"By bringing together complementary strengths in AI, language, knowledge, and intelligent computing, we envision trustworthy, inclusive and scalable AI technologies that can transform how people learn, work and access knowledge in India and across the world.”
Prof. Yogesh Simmhan, Professor in the Department of Computational and Data Sciences, IISc, noted: “The future of computing will be shaped by the convergence of hybrid cloud, AI agents and quantum technologies. IISc and IBM bring complementary research strengths to jointly explore intelligent, cloud-native platforms that can reason, adapt and orchestrate quantum-classical, edge AI and agentic workflows at scale, translating frontier ideas into trustworthy, sustainable technologies with real-world impact for India and the world.”
As IBM extends its collaborations with IIT Bombay and IISc into their next phases, the research agenda reflects the evolving needs of enterprise AI—from trusted and sovereign AI to quantum-centric supercomputing workflows and intelligent infrastructure.
By bringing together IBM’s expertise in AI, hybrid cloud and quantum computing with the academic excellence of two of India's leading research institutions, the collaborations aim to accelerate innovations that align with national goals, are scientifically rigorous, industry-relevant and designed for real-world impact.
Since the inception of these collaborations, IBM, IIT Bombay and IISc have worked together to advance research across artificial intelligence, hybrid cloud, distributed systems and quantum computing, while creating opportunities for students and researchers to tackle industry-inspired challenges.
As the collaborations enter their next phase, they will continue to foster interdisciplinary research, nurture the next generation of scientific talent and accelerate innovations that help shape the future of computing.

D-Wave Quantum Inc., a Palo Alto, Calif.-based quantum computing company, and the Supply Chain Management Research Center in the Sam M. Walton College of Business at the University of Arkansas are collaborating to explore quantum computing’s impact on complex supply chain problems.
According to a Monday (Oct. 5) news release, the collaboration establishes the Quantum Supply Chain Initiative Support Fund to advance thought leadership, education, and independent research on applying quantum computing to supply chain management across retail, transportation and national defense. D-Wave and the UA announced the collaboration Monday at CSCMP EDGE 2026, a four-day conference and exhibition hosted in Nashville, Tenn., by the Council of Supply Chain Management Professionals.
D-Wave has also joined the Supply Chain Management Research Center’s partnership program, which has more than 25 industry partners. A UA spokeswoman said D-Wave gave $50,000 for the initiative and will receive entitlements from the Supply Chain Management Research Center. Membership is year-to-year, and the gift is project-focused “instead of a cadenced amount.” A UA spokesman said the entitlements provide access to UA events and students.
According to D-Wave, it’s the first commercial supplier of quantum computers and the only one to offer dual-platform quantum computing products and services, spanning annealing and gate-model quantum computing technologies. According to IBM, quantum computing is an emergent field of computer science and engineering that uses quantum mechanics to solve problems faster than classical supercomputers.
The release shows that supply chain decision-making often requires organizations to coordinate routes, inventory, facilities, schedules and workforce while balancing cost, speed, service and resilience. Quantum and hybrid-quantum computing approaches are being implemented as networks grow more complex and disruptions become more consequential.
The collaboration between D-Wave and the Supply Chain Management Research Center is expected to explore quantum optimization research for a variety of supply chain use cases, including transportation routing, logistics network design, inventory and resource allocation, and scheduling and decision-making under disruption. The joint effort may also include curriculum and case development, student learning opportunities, industry engagement, government and academic stakeholders, and the development and sharing of practical frameworks and insights.
“Supply chains are highly dynamic, with decision-making that can have a far-reaching impact on efficiency and costs,” said Murray Thom, vice president of quantum technology evangelism at D-Wave. “We’re seeing quantum computing technologies emerge as potentially powerful alternatives to existing classical approaches. The Walton College is at the forefront of supply chain innovation, not only educating the next generation of supply chain professionals and conducting groundbreaking research but also engaging industry to effect economic change. We’re thrilled to support the college as it facilitates a quantum-ready supply chain.”
“The Walton College is dedicated to exploring the very latest methods, processes and technologies that advance supply chain management and resilience,” said Brian Fugate, associate dean for research and graduate programs at Walton College. “Quantum computing is showing great potential to help organizations accelerate decision-making, mitigate disruption and drive better operational outcomes. We’re excited to partner with D-Wave, one of the quantum computing industry’s foremost leaders, to bring quantum into our research portfolio and ultimately benefit students and partners alike.”

SuperQ Quantum targets the operating system layer as quantum computing turns commercial
Published: October 05, 2026 at 9:12a.m. EDT
An overview of SuperQ's technology stack, running from in-field decision-making up to the operating system layer that ties quantum and classical computing together.
Disseminated on behalf of:SuperQ Quantum Computing Inc.
SuperQ closed an oversubscribed C$4.6 million brokered placement led by Canaccord Genuity in June and reported roughly C$5 million in treasury against approximately 37 million shares outstanding.
SuperQ’s SuperPQC cybersecurity suite produced the company’s first major enterprise deal in post-quantum security in May, a commercial agreement to move NASDAQ-listed AI Financial Corporation’s payments and trading infrastructure onto quantum-resistant encryption.
Two government-backed programs opened within a week in July: selection into a Global Affairs Canada-supported U.S. defence accelerator, with a place at Fed Supernova 2026 in Austin, and Deep Tech Canada’s November Trade Mission to Barcelona.
Artificial intelligence has taught industry to predict. It has not taught industry to decide.
Most hard business problems are optimization problems: routing fleets, scheduling power across a grid, narrowing millions of molecular candidates down to the handful worth synthesizing. Classical computers can produce an answer. They cannot guarantee the best one.
Quantum computing can close part of that gap, but only in combination with the classical machines already doing the work. Almost no enterprise employs the specialists required to make the two operate together.
That is where SuperQ Quantum Computing Inc. (CSE: QBTQ | OTCQB: QBTQF | FSE: 25X) now finds itself.
The Calgary-based company sells the Super platform, a commercially available system that builds and runs hybrid quantum-classical solutions on a customer’s behalf. The platform’s two modules handle optimization and post-quantum cybersecurity.
Super OS, in development, is the orchestration layer designed to run that stack across data centres, on-site infrastructure, and third-party quantum hardware. Super Nova is the modular computer built to run Super OS natively. ChatQLM is a separate consumer app putting quantum-backed reasoning in a phone.
One argument runs through all of it: quantum computing scales commercially only when someone builds the layer that makes it usable.
“When you use your laptop, you use the CPU and GPU seamlessly through Windows or macOS or Linux,” said Founder and CEO Dr. Muhammad Ali Khan. “We are creating the same experience for quantum computing.”
Most quantum companies are selling something you cannot buy yet. SuperQ’s core product is already on the market.
The Super platform behaves less like software and more like staff. A customer describes a business problem in plain language. The platform breaks it down, decides which parts belong on classical hardware and which belong on a quantum processor, builds the solution, and returns results in the customer’s own vocabulary.
“The user doesn’t have to have expertise in computer science or physics,” Khan said. “They only focus on their problem domain and they let the platform do the work.”
Khan is deliberate about what is being sold. “We don’t sell technology. We sell value, and the value we sell is mathematical optimization. Quantum computing is just a tool.”
Security is the other half of the business
The technology that solves those problems also threatens the encryption protecting everything else. RSA-based cryptography secures most passwords and payments in use today, and is expected to weaken as quantum machines scale.
The deadlines are already being set. Google has committed to completing its post-quantum cryptography migration by 2029, a year ahead of the date the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has set to deprecate the current standards.
SuperPQC diagnoses that exposure and manages the migration. It is the module that produced the company’s first major enterprise deal in post-quantum security.
In May, SuperQ signed a commercial agreement with AI Financial Corporation (NASDAQ: AIFC), formerly ALT5 Sigma. The work covers securing the payments and trading infrastructure behind the client’s digital asset platform, and extends into AI and compute infrastructure.
“AI Financial is our first major enterprise deal in post-quantum cybersecurity,” Khan said.
The buyer put it in bigger terms. “By partnering with SuperQ, AI Financial is among the first to embark on the journey toward a quantum utility and security economy,” said Tony Isaac, CEO of AI Financial Corporation.
Why SuperQ says it does not have competitors
Investors comparing listed quantum names usually start with qubit counts. Khan argues that is the wrong scoreboard, because SuperQ is not trying to win it.
“Anyone who’s producing quantum hardware, we don’t see them as competitive,” he said. “We’re an enabler for other quantum companies.”
Super OS is designed to run on third-party quantum machines as readily as on SuperQ’s own. Every hardware maker that ships a machine becomes a potential channel rather than a threat.
That position also shapes what SuperQ is building itself. “We created the hardware because we saw that not everyone would want to buy a $50 million machine that does only one type of calculation,” Khan said.
We don’t sell technology. We sell value, and the value we sell is mathematical optimization.
— Dr. Muhammad Ali Khan, Founder and CEO of SuperQ Quantum Computing Inc.
Super Nova is where the software thesis becomes a hardware business. The machine is modular, combining superconducting quantum chips, GPUs, and control electronics, with customers taking only the stacks they need.
Development of this quantum hardware layer takes place at the University of Waterloo’s Digital Quantum Matter Lab, supervised by renowned superconducting quantum physics expert Professor Matteo Mariantoni. Leveraging Waterloo’s state-of-the-art clean room and advanced fabrication facilities enables rapid prototyping, device iteration, and seamless system integration, supporting a modular architecture designed to directly integrate with enterprise IT environments and significantly lower capital costs.
The commercial argument is cost. A quantum computer today typically runs US$20 million to US$50 million, Khan said, and performs one class of calculation. Super Nova is being targeted at under US$10 million.
“We can achieve a lot through our operating system by making a smaller number of qubits work with classical hardware,” he said.
The first on-premise deployment of Super OS is expected this fall, though no customer has been named. The first Super Nova unit is slated for the first half of 2027 and will be built in-house at the company’s manufacturing lab.
Two government-backed doors, one week apart
M1-qbtq-2026oct05-2 Recent milestones have landed SuperQ in front of government buyers on two continents.
July brought validation from an unusual direction.
SuperQ was selected into the Canada and Q-Branch Dual-Use Accelerator, backed by a formal agreement with Global Affairs Canada. The program put the company in front of U.S. defence and federal buyers through curated meetings, including three days at Fed Supernova 2026 in Austin from August 18–20.
“Our technology is of significant interest for dual-use purposes,” Khan said, pointing to six months of engagement with Canadian defence primes.
A week later came Europe. SuperQ was selected for Deep Tech Canada’s Trade Mission to Barcelona, exhibiting in the Canadian pavilion at the Smart City Expo World Congress in November.
The target application is urban optimization: transportation, logistics, and energy movement through congested networks.
Barcelona is a deliberate choice. The city hosts the €22 million Quantum Spain initiative and the €43 million Vall de la Quàntica program, concentrating public buyers in one place.
From curated meetings to a live exercise
On October 1, SuperQ received the evaluation report from a live military exercise at the Bush Combat Development Complex in Texas. The company tested Super Edge, its optimization platform for use on devices in the field, and was the only quantum firm and the only Canadian technology provider in the international cohort.
SuperQ says the report shows completion of all primary operational objectives, sustained performance under simulated network degradation, and integration with existing military command systems. The full report is published in a public repository.
“It was fantastic to see SuperQ as the only Canadian company participating in the international cohort of companies testing products at the Bush Combat Development Complex in a real test environment,” said Duane Robson, Consul and Senior Trade Commissioner at the Consulate General of Canada in Dallas.
A field test under contested conditions is a different order of proof than a commercial pilot.
To execute this vision, SuperQ has assembled a seasoned leadership and advisory team. Khan is a Silicon Valley entrepreneur and computer scientist with over 20 years of experience, and has scaled private and public companies across Canada, the U.S., and the UAE. A former academic trained at the University of Cambridge and the University of Calgary, he is a Vanier, Killam, and Commonwealth Scholar, and launched the ChatQLM app at CES 2026.
Chief Business Officer Manoj Joseph brings deep B2B enterprise sales and business development experience, having previously worked with major technology companies, including Eros, Smartron, and DLT Ledgers.
The team is further strengthened by Senior Strategic Advisor Bob Dameron. Formerly the Head of Business Development for the quantum unicorn Multiverse Computing, Dameron also brings decades of public markets experience from senior executive roles at the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX).
The capital structure is the quiet part of the story.
SuperQ carries roughly 37 million shares outstanding, a small float that gives existing shareholders more exposure to any commercial success.
The company reported roughly C$5 million in treasury after the June financing. Khan said the long enterprise sales cycles that produced few closed deals last year are now converting.
He said the goal is to balance burn against revenue by year-end. “Even if that doesn’t happen, we have a 12-month runway based on the cash position we have right now,” he said.
The next 12 months carry defined catalysts: the first on-premise Super OS deployment, the first Super Nova build, follow-through from the Texas exercise, and European entry through Barcelona.
For investors weighing quantum exposure, most listed names are a bet on a machine. SuperQ is a bet on the layer that machine will need to run.
About SuperQ Quantum Computing Inc.
SuperQ Quantum Computing Inc. (CSE: QBTQ | OTCQB: QBTQF | FSE: 25X) is building the operating system, Super OS™, to unify quantum and supercomputing for data centre and enterprise deployment. This OS will run on SuperQ’s in-development Super Nova™ hybrid quantum computers and third-party hardware. The company’s already commercialized Super™ platform enables enterprises, government, and research institutions to autonomously solve complex optimization and cybersecurity challenges by combining quantum and high-performance computing. The company is also putting quantum computing in the palm of consumers’ hands through ChatQLM™ - the world’s first consumer application powered by hybrid quantum and supercomputing.

DOE Wants Quantum Computing Judged by Science, Not Qubit Counts
The U.S. Department of Energy has outlined a three-phase roadmap aimed at advancing scientifically useful, error-corrected quantum computing. Image: Generated via ChatGPT. has outlined a three-phase roadmap aimed at advancing scientifically useful, error-corrected quantum computing. Image: Generated via ChatGPT.

The U.S. Department of Energy wants quantum computers judged by the science they deliver, not the qubits they count. A federal advisory committee has now laid out a three-phase plan to get there, and DOE paired it with a competition worth up to $215 million for private companies.
The plan, titled "Path to an Integrated Quantum Future", came from a Scientific Computing Advisory Committee subcommittee chaired by Anna Grassellino, Fermilab's chief technology officer. The quantum computing roadmap targets a scientifically relevant, error-corrected quantum computer by 2028. DOE unveiled it on Sept. 17, and Fermilab highlighted it on Sept. 25.
It signals where federal money will likely flow. The catch is that the plan is less specific than the competition built around it.
What Is in DOE's Three-Phase Plan?
I: Quantum Grand Challenges2026 to 2028Competitions pair national labs, universities, and industry.Scientifically relevant, error-corrected capability by 2028.
II: DOE Quantum Computing User FacilityAfter Phase IAn open, collaborative scientific instrument.Timing, scale, and scope subject to "careful evaluation".
III: Integrated Quantum Future2030 and beyondQuantum co-processors join DOE's AI and supercomputing systems.Quantum computing increasingly integrated across DOE science.
Sources: SCAC report, Fermilab.
Supratik Guha, a University of Chicago professor of molecular engineering, served as vice chair. Its science targets include catalyst chemistry, superconducting materials, fusion-relevant materials, and the quantum field theories behind particle physics.
The plan is also technology neutral. The report cites broad consensus that it is premature to converge on a single technological pathway. DARPA is running its own comparison, and evaluators can now test Microsoft's Majorana 2 chip hands-on at a University of Maryland facility.
How the Quantum Genesis Q Competition Fits
Darío Gil, DOE's under secretary for science, wrote, "Our goal is not simply to build the largest quantum computer; it is to solve problems that are otherwise completely intractable."
The Quantum Genesis Q Competition is open to private companies, with final applications due Oct. 19. Its structure:
Phase I: Up to $1.5 million per awardee for early milestones
Phase II: A $100 million pool for awardees that demonstrate a system with at least 100 logical qubits
Bonus pools: Two $50 million pools, at 150 and 200 logical qubits
Testbed call: A separate $45 million verification and validation call for national labs
The money follows $300 million in CHIPS Act awards that Commerce finalized in September for PsiQuantum, Quantinuum, and Rigetti. Those funds support manufacturing and scaling. DOE pays for demonstrated logical qubits.
The structure makes the distinction important: the roadmap defines the scientific destination, while the competition uses logical-qubit milestones to decide where near-term funding goes.
What eWeek Found: The Roadmap Preaches Utility, but the Payout Counts Qubits
Gil wrote that "success must be measured by scientific utility." The competition's largest rewards, however, turn on logical qubit counts. That is a hardware metric. The testbed call may be where utility gets checked, but it is not yet clear how DOE will score a result as scientifically relevant.
The numbers also sit far apart. The competition's minimum is 100 logical qubits. On page 23, the report says "approximately 1,000 logical qubits and sustained fault-tolerant operation" would enable a user facility after 2028.
On page 32, it says the facility's timing, scale, and scope "require careful evaluation as quantum technologies and scientific applications mature." Phase II therefore looks like a judgment call.
Three things will show whether DOE’s roadmap is working: which companies enter the competition, how national-lab testbeds define and verify “scientifically relevant” results, and whether any team can demonstrate useful fault-tolerant performance by 2028 rather than simply hitting a qubit threshold.
The roadmap’s central test is therefore not whether quantum computers get larger. It is whether DOE can turn hardware progress into scientific capability that justifies moving from experiments to a shared user facility.

How AI, Machine Learning and Quantum Computing Could Transform Product Development – IT Voice
AI, ML and Quantum Computing in Product Development
Product development has always depended on understanding customers, testing ideas and making informed decisions. What is changing is the amount of technology involved in each stage. Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML) and, over time, quantum computing are opening new possibilities for how products are researched, designed, tested and improved.
For product managers, engineers and business leaders, understanding these technologies is becoming increasingly useful. The goal is not to replace human judgement, but to give teams better tools for solving complex problems and making decisions based on richer information.
AI can support product teams across several stages of the development lifecycle. Instead of relying entirely on manual research and analysis, teams can use AI to process large volumes of information and identify patterns.
For example, AI can help analyse:
Support queries and recurring complaints
Generative AI can also assist with brainstorming, creating prototypes, preparing product documentation and exploring different design concepts. Human expertise remains important because AI-generated ideas still need to be checked for accuracy, practicality and relevance.
Machine learning allows systems to learn patterns from historical data and use those patterns to make predictions or classifications. In product development, this can be particularly useful when teams have access to substantial amounts of customer or operational data.
ML models can identify trends in customer behaviour that may not be obvious through manual analysis. Product teams can use these insights when deciding which features deserve further investigation.
Machine learning can help detect unusual patterns during testing and highlight potential problems earlier. In manufacturing and technology products, predictive models can also contribute to quality control and maintenance planning.
Recommendation engines and personalised interfaces are already common examples of machine learning in digital products. As organisations collect better data, similar approaches can be applied to other areas of customer experience.
Professionals looking to build a stronger foundation in these technologies may explore an AI and machine learning course for professionals to understand how AI and ML concepts can be applied in practical business and product environments.
Quantum computing is at a different stage of development from mainstream AI and ML. It uses quantum mechanical principles to approach certain computational problems in fundamentally different ways.
Its potential relevance to product development comes from problems that involve extremely large numbers of possible combinations.
Product teams often need to balance multiple variables, such as cost, materials, manufacturing capacity, delivery routes and performance requirements. Quantum computing could eventually contribute to solving some highly complex optimisation problems more efficiently.
Another potential application is simulation. Quantum computers may eventually help researchers model certain molecular and material behaviours that are difficult to represent using conventional computers.
This could have implications for areas such as pharmaceuticals, advanced materials, energy and electronics.
A Quantum Computing and Machine Learning Course can help professionals understand the relationship between these two fields and where quantum approaches may fit into future technology strategies.
Bringing AI, ML and Quantum Computing Together
These technologies should not necessarily be viewed as competing alternatives. They may eventually work alongside conventional computing and one another.
A possible product development workflow could involve:
AI collecting and organising customer and market information.
Machine learning identifying patterns and generating predictive insights.
Human teams evaluating ideas against business and customer requirements.
Quantum computing, where technically appropriate, addressing highly complex optimisation or simulation problems.
AI and ML helping teams interpret results and improve the product.
The practical value will depend heavily on the problem being solved, the quality of available data and the maturity of the technology.
How to Choose the Right Executive Education Programme
Professionals considering executive education should look beyond the course title. The right programme depends on their current role, technical background and learning objectives.
Consider these factors:
Curriculum: Check whether it covers concepts you can actually use in your work.
Technical depth: Decide whether you need strategic understanding or hands-on technical knowledge.
Business relevance: Look for practical applications, case studies and real-world examples.
Learning format: Consider whether the schedule works alongside professional responsibilities.
Institution and faculty: Review the academic background and industry experience involved.
Peer learning: Executive programmes can provide opportunities to learn from professionals working in different industries.
The best fit is generally the programme that matches your existing knowledge and the type of problems you want to solve.
The increasing use of advanced technology does not mean every product professional needs to become a data scientist or quantum computing researcher. However, understanding the fundamentals can make collaboration with technical teams much easier.
Product leaders should become comfortable discussing:
This combination of business understanding and technology awareness can help teams ask better questions when evaluating new product opportunities.
1. How can AI help product development?
AI can support research, customer feedback analysis, ideation, documentation, prototyping and other activities. Its usefulness depends on the quality of the information and human oversight.
2. What is the difference between AI and machine learning?
AI is the broader field of creating systems that perform tasks associated with human intelligence. Machine learning is a subset of AI that enables systems to learn patterns from data.
3. Will quantum computing replace traditional computers?
There is no reason to expect quantum computers to replace conventional computers for everyday computing. Their potential lies mainly in specialised problems where quantum approaches may offer advantages.
4. Do product managers need to learn quantum computing?
Not necessarily. A basic understanding can be useful for professionals working in technology-intensive industries, particularly when assessing future applications and opportunities.
5. Why is executive education useful for technology professionals?
Executive education can help professionals connect technical concepts with business decisions, product strategy and organisational challenges while continuing their careers.
AI and machine learning are already influencing how organisations understand customers, analyse data and develop products. Quantum computing remains an evolving technology, but its potential applications in optimisation, simulation and complex problem-solving make it worth watching.
For product professionals, the key is not simply learning every new technology. It is understanding where these tools can create practical value, recognising their limitations and knowing how to combine technological capabilities with sound product thinking.

Quantum computing has a huge market opportunity that's quickly approaching. Many in the industry now project 2029 as the year viable quantum computing technology arrives, which isn't all that far away. Companies of all sizes are vying for viable quantum computing technology, including some of the largest in the world. At the same time, several upstarts are attempting to capture market share, and this new technology has the potential to create several incredible new companies.
One of the brightest quantum computing upstarts is IonQ (IONQ -1.83%). IonQ is taking a different approach to quantum computing than its peers, and it's looking very promising. Another major competitor is Alphabet (GOOG +1.02%) (GOOGL +0.86%), the world's third-largest company.
These two are completely different sizes and have different return levels, but which is the better investment?
Image source: Getty Images.
There are multiple pathways for quantum computing
Quantum computing is more of a concept than an established technique. The general idea is to use a particle's movements to perform calculations, but how that particle is controlled varies from company to company. Companies are trying different approaches to best control particles for calculations, ranging from superconducting computing (like Alphabet) to trapped ion (IonQ). Each approach has its own strengths and weaknesses, but it ultimately boils down to two factors: speed and accuracy.
Alphabet is taking an approach that optimizes speed over accuracy. The idea here is that, eventually, the technology will become accurate enough that faster processing speeds will be more attractive to clients.

IonQ's approach optimizes for accuracy and is working on processing speed by adding more qubits, the quantum computing equivalent of bits. While its approach may be slower, sheer size can make up for it.
Nobody knows which technique will ultimately win, so investing in companies with a variety of approaches makes the most sense. However, one company has much more to gain than the other.
With IonQ's only business being quantum computing, it must produce a viable product or go bankrupt. While that life-or-death comparison may seem a bit stark, it's the reality for an upstart like IonQ. Fortunately, it has several partners and is nearing production of its 256-qubit system, which could be the first viable early-stage quantum computing product ever released.
If that product sees strong adoption, the market may get on board with IonQ's prospects and send its stock skyrocketing. Since it's a relatively small $16 billion company, it wouldn't take much of a boost to send its stock skyrocketing. It could deliver multi-bagger returns over the long run if it can take significant market share.

Alphabet is different. If its quantum computing product lineup doesn't pan out and goes bust, the stock really wouldn't be affected. It would still proceed with its normal plan to produce incredible AI products and dominate the online search industry. While it may have missed an opportunity to provide leading quantum computing units for its cloud computing business, it will still be a strong investment.
Even if it does develop a viable quantum computing product, there are questions as to how much it will actually affect Alphabet's financial picture. During the second quarter, Alphabet generated nearly $120 billion in revenue.
An additional $1 billion in revenue doesn't really move the needle for Alphabet. However, it would mean the world to IonQ and its shareholders.
So, if you're looking for ultimate upside, but with high risk, IonQ is the better quantum computing stock pick. However, if you're looking for guaranteed positive returns and little risk with some quantum computing exposure, Alphabet is the better stock pick of the two.

Here's How Quantum Computing's EQC Approach Supports Growth
Quantum Computing Inc. QUBT or QCi is advancing its quantum computing strategy through Entropy Quantum Computing ("EQC"). Traditional quantum systems rely on costly error correction and highly controlled environments, while EQC uses quantum entropy and decoherence as resources for computation. This approach could reduce the need for cryogenic cooling and isolation while enabling integrated photonic systems designed for greater scalability and operational flexibility.
Leveraging the EQC approach, QCi's Dirac-3 platform is a third-generation, rack-mountable system designed to solve complex, real-world optimization problems at room temperature. The platform reflects QCi's focus on applying EQC to practical computing applications without relying on the highly controlled environments typically associated with conventional quantum systems.
Further supporting the development and adoption of its quantum technology, QCi signed a three-year Framework Agreement with Hamad Bin Khalifa University ("HBKU") in Qatar. Under the agreement, QCi will provide HBKU with cloud-based access to the Dirac-3 system, along with an installation in Qatar to support the country's quantum ecosystem and regional leadership.
Quantum Technologies Used by QUBT's Peers
IonQ's IONQ commercialization thesis remains tied to technical milestones that can move IonQ from prototype systems toward repeatable semiconductor-based deployments. By the second quarter of 2026, IonQ had progressed through three rounds of tape-outs for its first semiconductor quantum chip and received 256-qubit prototypes, which met the critical quality metrics required for production-grade systems. IONQ also reported key elements of its walking-cat architecture and quantum error-correction work on a Tempo engineering system.
Rigetti's RGTI superconducting qubit platform is built around an in-house modular chiplet design intended to scale systems without relying on ever-larger monolithic processors. Its 36-qubit Cepheus system uses four 9-qubit chiplets, while Cepheus-1-108Q uses 12 interconnected 9-qubit chiplets and became generally available in April 2026.
The 108-qubit system is currently operating at about 99.1% median two-qubit gate fidelity, 99.9% median single-qubit fidelity and gate speeds near 60 nanoseconds. Quantum Computing Inc. to Showcase Quantum Secure Communications Beyond Quantum Key Distribution at ECOC 2026
First-time live demonstration combines quantum encryption and authentication on a single platform, alongside quantum key distribution and advanced instrumentation for secure optical communications
HOBOKEN, N.J., Sept. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Quantum Computing Inc. ("QCi" or the "Company") (Nasdaq: QUBT), a vertically integrated quantum company pioneering photonics and semiconductor manufacturing, today announced it will showcase, for the first time, an integrated quantum security platform that brings encryption and authentication together in a single solution, at the ECOC Exhibition 2026, September 21–23 at FYCMA in Málaga, Spain. At Booth #1436, QCi will demonstrate live quantum communication solutions leveraging time-frequency and polarization-based approaches, highlighting how quantum technologies are moving from research and development toward practical solutions for securing the communications infrastructure of the future.
As organizations prepare for the post-quantum era, the challenge is no longer understanding the value of quantum-secure communications, but overcoming the barriers that have limited deployment. Traditional QKD systems often face challenges associated with scalability, operational complexity, infrastructure cost, and dependence on classical authentication methods. As a result, many quantum communication technologies have remained confined to specialized research environments.
QCi's entanglement-based quantum security platform is designed to overcome these limitations by bringing two critical elements of secure communications - encryption and authentication - together on a single platform. For the first time, QCi will showcase an integrated quantum security solution that combines quantum key distribution (QKD) with hardware-based Quantum Identity Authentication (QIA), demonstrating how quantum technologies can address both the secure exchange of encryption keys and the fundamental need to establish trusted identities between communicating parties.
The platform combines high-dimensional quantum key distribution, direct entanglement verification, Quantum Identity Authentication (QIA), and integrated key management in a telecom-compatible architecture. QIA is based on QCi's patented invention, "Systems and Methods for Quantum-Secured, Private-Preserving Computations," which was granted patent protection in the United States and more than 40 other countries and was recognized with the 44th Edison Patent Award, presented to Dr. Yuping Huang and Dr. Lac Nguyen for their contributions to quantum-secured, privacy-preserving computing. The patented technology enables quantum authentication and verification of private information without requiring that information to be shared, addressing security vulnerabilities beyond encryption alone. By reducing dependence on classical authentication, supporting wavelength-multiplexed scaling across multiple nodes, and operating in a compact room-temperature form factor, QCi is advancing a practical path toward deployable quantum-secure networking infrastructure.
QCi is addressing that challenge with technologies designed to bring quantum security into practical communications environments.
At ECOC, QCi will feature the following at Booth #1436:
Flexible Quantum Instrumentation & Metrology
QCi will demonstrate a highly adaptable platform for quantum measurement, characterization and system development. The platform is designed to help researchers, developers and engineers to understand, test and validate quantum technologies and concepts, supporting next generation quantum applications, and transitioning laboratory concepts toward practical systems.
QCi will showcase an integrated solution combining Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) with hardware-based Quantum Identity Authentication (QIA). QIA leverages QCi's Quantum Zero-Knowledge Proof (QZKP) technology to provide quantum-safe authentication without relying solely on computational cryptography.
QCi will also showcase its advanced photonics components, highlighting the critical building blocks that enable next-generation quantum and optical communications systems and underscoring the Company's vertically integrated approach to photonics technology and manufacturing.
Together, these technologies demonstrate a more comprehensive approach to quantum-secured communications by addressing both the secure exchange of cryptographic keys and the fundamental need to establish trust between communicating parties.
"The transition to quantum-secure communications is no longer a long-term technology discussion. Organizations are beginning to consider what it will take to protect communications and critical data against the quantum and AI threat," said Yong Meng Sua, Chief Technology Officer of QCi. "At ECOC, we're showing what the future can look like in practice. Our demonstrations bring together quantum authentication, quantum key distribution and the instrumentation required to develop and validate quantum systems, giving the telecomm industry a firsthand look at how quantum technologies can strengthen the security of tomorrow's communications."
Quantum-Authenticated Communications for Broad Security Applications
QCi will also participate in the ECOC Product Focus Theatre with a presentation exploring the role of quantum authentication in securing communications across a broad range of applications. Titled "The Quantum Secure Solution: Quantum-authenticated communications for broad applications in security," the presentation will take place on Wednesday, September 23, from 14:50 to 15:10 and will be delivered by Massimo Di Blasio, Director, Product Line Management/Business Development at QCi.
The presentation will examine how quantum-authenticated communications can provide new approaches to establishing identity and trust in secure communications systems as organizations prepare for the evolving quantum threat.
"Optical communications form the foundation of the connected world, and security has to evolve alongside the networks themselves," said Sua. "Quantum technologies have the potential to fundamentally change how we establish trust and protect information. ECOC gives us an opportunity to demonstrate that potential through technologies that are being developed with real-world applications in mind."

Quantum Computing Inc. (Nasdaq: QUBT) is a vertically integrated quantum company pioneering photonics and semiconductor manufacturing, and delivering accessible, scalable, and cost-effective quantum machines, photonics products, and advanced packaging. The Company provides foundry services for photonic chips and semiconductor manufacturing and offers a vertically integrated portfolio spanning photonics and electronic components, subsystems, and full-stack systems.
Designed to operate at room-temperature with low-power requirements, QCi's technologies enable practical deployment across high-growth markets, including high-performance computing, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, aerospace and defense, and advanced sensing and imaging.
Headquartered in Hoboken, New Jersey, QCi also has operations in Arizona, California, Illinois, Indiana, Massachusetts, North Carolina and Virginia. By combining advanced materials, device engineering, and scalable manufacturing, QCi delivers integrated quantum, photonics, and semiconductor technologies, accelerating commercialization and real-world adoption.

RGTI vs QUBT: Which Quantum Computing Stock Has More Upside Potential?
The quantum computing race is no longer just about who can build the most powerful machine. It is increasingly becoming a contest between companies pursuing different paths to commercial adoption while convincing investors they can turn breakthrough technology into sustainable businesses.
That contrast was on full display during the latest earnings season as Rigetti Computing RGTI and Quantum Computing Inc. QUBT outlined sharply different strategies for scaling their businesses. Rigetti doubled down on its superconducting quantum computing roadmap, highlighting progress on its 108-qubit Cepheus-1 system, a modular chiplet architecture aimed at 1,000-qubit systems and growing government-backed initiatives. Meanwhile, QUBT leaned into its room-temperature photonic platform, expanding through acquisitions, semiconductor manufacturing and AI-focused photonics products designed to generate commercial revenue alongside its long-term quantum ambitions.
Both companies reported second-quarter revenues above $5 million, but the drivers behind those results looked very different. Rigetti's 185% revenue jump was fueled by quantum hardware deployments, while QUBT's 9,000% surge reflected contributions from its rapidly expanding photonics and semiconductor businesses. With both stocks competing for investor attention in one of the market's fastest-evolving industries, the bigger question is which execution strategy appears stronger based on their latest updates.
Let's get into more detail.
Rigetti's second-quarter results reinforced an execution-driven investment case as revenues jumped 185% year over year to $5.1 million, fueled by on-premises Novera QPU sales, while gross margin expanded to 43% from 31% a year ago.
Beyond the financials, the company continued advancing its 108-qubit Cepheus-1 platform, reaffirmed its chiplet-based roadmap toward roughly 1,000 qubits over the next three years, strengthened its government ties through a U.S. Department of Commerce letter of intent for up to $100 million in potential CHIPS Act funding and ended the quarter with $541.3 million in cash, cash equivalents and investments and no debt.
Rigetti's biggest challenge remains converting technical milestones into durable commercial scale. Although revenues grew sharply, quarterly sales remain relatively modest at $5.1 million, while operating expenses climbed to $30.3 million as the company continued investing heavily in R&D, chip design, fabrication and refrigeration infrastructure to support higher-qubit systems.
At the same time, management still needs to deliver meaningful improvements in Cepheus-1's gate fidelity and coherence times before progressing toward its 1,000-qubit ambitions, while the proposed CHIPS Act funding remains contingent on a definitive agreement and customary approvals.
Quantum Computing's second quarter highlighted a broader commercialization strategy that extends beyond quantum computing alone. Revenues surged to $5.6 million from just $61,000 a year ago, with contributions from government, commercial and educational customers across its photonics portfolio.
The company accelerated its expansion through the acquisitions of NHanced Semiconductors, Luminar Semiconductor and NuCrypt, strengthening its advanced packaging and semiconductor manufacturing capabilities while launching its Fab 2 initiative.
Commercial traction also improved with the rollout of the NeuraWave photonic AI platform, the installation of a DIRAC-3 optimization system at a global consulting firm, a multi-unit NeuraWave framework agreement with Planck Dynamics and a contract backlog that reached $42.5 million, backed by a cash and investment position of roughly $1.3 billion.
QUBT's rapid expansion also brings meaningful execution risks as the company integrates multiple acquisitions while scaling manufacturing and commercialization simultaneously. Operating expenses more than doubled to $21.8 million, due to higher R&D spending, personnel costs, sales and marketing investments and acquisition-related expenses.
The company remains heavily dependent on government-funded work, with management indicating that roughly 70%-80% of current business comes from government subcontracting, while contract timing remains lumpy and backlog is expected to be recognized over 12 to 18 months rather than translating into immediate revenue.
In addition, management is evaluating another $50-$100 million of potential investment to enhance NHanced's manufacturing capabilities, adding another layer of capital deployment and integration complexity.

Final Take: RGTI or QUBT?
The latest earnings season highlighted two very different execution stories. QUBT paired revenue growth with expanding commercial traction through acquisitions, a growing photonics business, a $42.5 million backlog and a sizeable $1.3 billion cash position, while Rigetti's quarter centered on advancing its superconducting roadmap, government partnerships and long-term technology milestones. Analyst sentiment also reflects a wider upside outlook for QUBT, with its average price target implying 103.8% upside from recent levels compared with 79.1% for Rigetti.
The two stocks entered the next phase with different outlooks. QUBT currently carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold), reflecting a more balanced near-term earnings outlook, while Rigetti carries a Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell), indicating weaker earnings expectations. Although QUBT appears better positioned from a commercialization and analyst-sentiment standpoint, both companies remain high-risk plays in an emerging industry where execution, customer adoption and technology milestones will likely remain the key factors to watch.

HOBOKEN, N.J., Oct. 1, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Quantum Computing Inc. ("QCi" or the "Company") (Nasdaq: QUBT), a vertically integrated quantum systems company pioneering photonics and semiconductor manufacturing, today announced Dirac-3S, the next-generation of its Dirac-3 quantum optimization machine, marking a significant step toward commercial deployment of QCi's quantum optimization technology.
Dirac-3S advances the platform across three areas – Speed, Scale and Solutions – with faster performance, improved solution quality, increased computing capacity and a modular architecture designed to support customers as their requirements grow. The first customer shipment of Dirac-3S is expected in November 2026.
Speed. Scale. Solutions.
Speed: Dirac-3S is engineered to efficiently solve increasingly complex optimization problems, with practical computation times demonstrated on problems involving up to 9,980 variables while consistently finding the optimal solution. This enables customers to tackle larger problems and explore more possibilities in less time.
Scale: Dirac-3S features a modular architecture designed to scale with customer requirements. The compact 5U base system can be extended with Expansion Modules to support larger and more complex optimization problems, with QCi demonstrating configurations supporting up to 9,980 variables with one Expansion Module. The architecture is designed to accommodate additional Expansion Modules, enabling customers to expand their system as their optimization needs grow. QCi has also advanced the Dirac-3S hardware architecture, manufacturing processes and supply chain to support increased production volumes, consistent product quality and broader commercial deployment. These improvements include enhanced error correction, component control and operational reliability.
Solutions: Dirac-3S is designed to address a broad range of real-world optimization problems on a single platform, through multiple optimization approaches including continuous, integer and higher-order optimization. QCi's latest error-correction techniques are designed to improve solution quality across applications in financial services, logistics and supply chains, manufacturing, energy, telecommunications, scientific research, and aerospace and defense.
The platform can be deployed on-premises or in the cloud and integrated into AI/ML pipelines, enabling organizations to incorporate quantum optimization into existing computational workflows.
"Dirac-3S takes our quantum optimization platform from demonstrating what is possible to delivering a system built for practical commercial use," said Yong Meng Sua, Chief Technology Officer of QCi. "We have increased performance and computing capacity, expanded the size and complexity of problems the system can address through a modular architecture, and advanced the hardware and manufacturing architecture needed to support broader deployment. This gives customers a flexible path to adopt quantum optimization and scale their computing capacity as their needs grow."
Dirac-3S builds on QCi's first-generation Dirac-3 quantum optimization machine, which has been used by academic researchers exploring quantum optimization algorithms and applications.
"Our experience with the first-generation Dirac-3 quantum optimization machine validated its potential as a powerful tool for solving meaningful optimization problems. QCi's continued innovation with the Dirac-3S, including its expanded computational capabilities, enables us to pursue significantly larger and more complex optimization challenges. We look forward to exploring new research directions and accelerating the development of practical, high-impact applications," said Professor Paul Griffin, Associate Professor, Singapore Management University.
QCi has published a new Technical Review evaluating Dirac-3S across synthetic, graph-based and industry-standard optimization benchmarks, including comparisons with Projected Gradient Descent and commercial classical solver Hexaly. Artificial intelligence has taught industry to predict. It has not taught industry to decide.
Most hard business problems are optimization problems: routing fleets, scheduling power across a grid, narrowing millions of molecular candidates down to the handful worth synthesizing. Classical computers can produce an answer. They cannot guarantee the best one.
Quantum computing can close part of that gap, but only in combination with the classical machines already doing the work. Almost no enterprise employs the specialists required to make the two operate together.
That is where SuperQ Quantum Computing Inc. (CSE: QBTQ | OTCQB: QBTQF | FSE: 25X) now finds itself.
The Calgary-based company sells the Super platform, a commercially available system that builds and runs hybrid quantum-classical solutions on a customer’s behalf. The platform’s two modules handle optimization and post-quantum cybersecurity.
Super OS, in development, is the orchestration layer designed to run that stack across data centres, on-site infrastructure, and third-party quantum hardware. One argument runs through all of it: quantum computing scales commercially only when someone builds the layer that makes it usable.
“When you use your laptop, you use the CPU and GPU seamlessly through Windows or macOS or Linux,” said Founder and CEO Dr. Muhammad Ali Khan. “We are creating the same experience for quantum computing.”
Most quantum companies are selling something you cannot buy yet. SuperQ’s core product is already on the market.
The Super platform behaves less like software and more like staff. A customer describes a business problem in plain language. The platform breaks it down, decides which parts belong on classical hardware and which belong on a quantum processor, builds the solution, and returns results in the customer’s own vocabulary.
“The user doesn’t have to have expertise in computer science or physics,” Khan said. “They only focus on their problem domain and they let the platform do the work.”
Khan is deliberate about what is being sold. “We don’t sell technology. We sell value, and the value we sell is mathematical optimization. Quantum computing is just a tool.”
Security is the other half of the business
The technology that solves those problems also threatens the encryption protecting everything else. RSA-based cryptography secures most passwords and payments in use today, and is expected to weaken as quantum machines scale.
The deadlines are already being set. Google has committed to completing its post-quantum cryptography migration by 2029, a year ahead of the date the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has set to deprecate the current standards.
SuperPQC diagnoses that exposure and manages the migration. It is the module that produced the company’s first major enterprise deal in post-quantum security.
In May, SuperQ signed a commercial agreement with AI Financial Corporation (NASDAQ: AIFC), formerly ALT5 Sigma. The work covers securing the payments and trading infrastructure behind the client’s digital asset platform, and extends into AI and compute infrastructure.
“AI Financial is our first major enterprise deal in post-quantum cybersecurity,” Khan said.
The buyer put it in bigger terms. “By partnering with SuperQ, AI Financial is among the first to embark on the journey toward a quantum utility and security economy,” said Tony Isaac, CEO of AI Financial Corporation.
Why SuperQ says it does not have competitors
Investors comparing listed quantum names usually start with qubit counts. Khan argues that is the wrong scoreboard, because SuperQ is not trying to win it.
“Anyone who’s producing quantum hardware, we don’t see them as competitive,” he said. “We’re an enabler for other quantum companies.”
Super OS is designed to run on third-party quantum machines as readily as on SuperQ’s own. Every hardware maker that ships a machine becomes a potential channel rather than a threat.
That position also shapes what SuperQ is building itself. “We created the hardware because we saw that not everyone would want to buy a $50 million machine that does only one type of calculation,” Khan said.

The commercial argument is cost. A quantum computer today typically runs US$20 million to US$50 million, Khan said, and performs one class of calculation. Super Nova is being targeted at under US$10 million.
“We can achieve a lot through our operating system by making a smaller number of qubits work with classical hardware,” he said.

The U.S. Department of Energy has outlined a three-phase roadmap aimed at advancing scientifically useful, error-corrected quantum computing.
